court: Court of Civil Appeals of Texas, El Paso
holding_summary: A hotel guest who had occupied a room on a day-to-day (and usually weekly) basis for about sixteen months was put out and his belongings moved to the lobby without judicial process; the court held the eviction lawful because a room let by a hotel from day to day is not a wartime 'housing accommodation' and an innkeeper may eject a guest on reasonable notice without resort to legal process. Finding no violation of a legal right, the court reversed the plaintiff's judgment and rendered judgment for the hotel proprietor.

quotes.text: since public inns are conducted for travelers and transient persons, it is not the duty of the innkeeper to keep one who has lost that status; that a person is not entitled to stay indefinitely, and on reasonable notice may be ejected without any other reason
did not construe and apply it as applicable to a hotel letting its accommodations from day to day on a daily basis and that under such circumstances an eviction was permissible
It is our conclusion, therefore, there has been no violation of a legal right and hence there can be no recoverable damage.

notes: Plaintiff took the room 'on a day basis at $1.75 per day and usually paid weekly' over ~16 months; classified duration as 'weeks' to reflect the actual recurring pattern even though the court's legal test turned on the day-to-day rate.

court: Court of Civil Appeals of Texas, Austin
holding_summary: A city amended its zoning ordinance to rezone two blocks in an established residential district to permit construction of a tourist camp of twenty-five to thirty cottages with an attached recreational and refreshment area. The court held the rezoning unreasonable and invalid because conditions in the district had not changed since the original 1945 zoning plan, and the record showed the change would increase traffic hazards, diminish residential privacy, and reduce property values without offsetting public benefit.

quotes.text: if the amendatory ordinance is upheld the hazards of traffic in the area will be increased, that the existing privacy and quietness of the area will be diminished and that the value of the properties located there will decrease
The judgment of the trial court is reversed and judgment is here rendered declaring the amendatory ordinance invalid in so far as it relates to Blocks 5110 and 5113.

notes: characterization left null: the court adjudicates zoning validity only and never characterizes the guest occupancy itself as lease/license/lodging/innkeeping. duration_of_occupancy left unclear for the same reason — no facts about actual guest stays are in the record, only the permissibility of the land use.

court: Court of Civil Appeals of Texas, Texarkana
holding_summary: A homeowner let a room, and later the house, to an occupant for weekly payment; on an insurance-policy dispute over whether occupancy had changed from 'owner' to 'tenant,' the court held no landlord-tenant relationship arose because the homeowner retained a key and right of entry and left furniture, clothing, and kitchen utensils in the house, so the occupant lacked the exclusive possession essential to a tenancy. The court treated this as a question of law despite the parties' own use of the word 'rent.'

quotes.text: Even though Johnson used the word “rent” in describing his transaction with Singleton, it was within the province of the court to pass upon the significance in its relation to the facts adduced.
Singleton did not have the exclusive possession of the house and premises, which is an essential element in the creation of a tenancy status.
He was giving me a $1 a week when I was there, but I decided to rent him the house, and he was supposed to pay me $3.00 per week.

notes: Arises in a fire-insurance coverage dispute (owner- vs. tenant-occupancy clause), but the court's reasoning directly applies classic license-vs-lease/exclusive-possession doctrine to a householder's letting of a room and then the whole house.
